did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with a person dwelling in the shelter of the Most High and resting in the shadow of the Almighty—two images of refuge and protection.
The second verse contains a direct declaration of trust: the LORD is described as the speaker’s refuge and fortress, the God in whom he trusts.
Deliverance is described as protection from two kinds of danger: a hidden snare and a deadly pestilence.
The verse combines images of parental and military protection: a person takes refuge under the LORD’s wings, while His faithfulness is described as a shield and protective armor.
The psalm lists fears that arise at different times: terror by night, an arrow flying by day, a pestilence moving in darkness, and a destruction raging at noon.
The numbers “a thousand” and “ten thousand” emphasize the scale of the danger and contrast the fall of many around the person with the promise: “it will not come near you.”
This verse returns to the idea of refuge from the opening: the person has made the LORD his refuge and the Most High his dwelling place.
The LORD commands His angels to guard the person “in all your ways”; the next verse also describes this protection as carrying him in their hands.
The verse portrays victory over dangers represented by the lion, cobra, young lion, and serpent, using verbs of trampling and crushing.

In the final three verses, the voice changes to speech in the LORD’s own name. The promises are addressed to the one who loves Him and knows His name: an answer, His presence in trouble, deliverance, honor, salvation, and long life.
